title: 🗳️ Buy a Vote: How DAOs Get Robbed Overnight
ig_caption:
Stop scrolling—this is how “governance” gets weaponized. 🔥
Buy a vote, rob the treasury, and override the DAO.

• An attacker uses a governance token strategy to influence outcomes
• They “buy a vote” for PROPOSAL #42
• The malicious proposal instructs: send the entire treasury to 0xBAD…
• Voting power is calculated from tokens held at the snapshot block
• If you control enough tokens at snapshot time, your vote counts (e.g., 2.0M)
• “0 votes” happens when participants aren’t counted in the snapshot window

Practical takeaway: Many DAOs are vulnerable when voting power can be temporarily acquired or flash-injected around the snapshot. The fix is usually stronger token-weighting rules, anti-sybil measures, and timelocks with safety checks.

What should DAOs prioritize more: fast governance or snapshot fairness? 👇 Debate it in the comments.

fb_caption:
A DAO governance attack is essentially an “access control failure” dressed up as decentralization.

What the animation shows (on-chain mechanics):
• PROPOSAL #42 is submitted with a malicious action: send the entire treasury to an attacker-controlled address (0xBAD…)
• Voting uses snapshot-based voting power: voting power = tokens held at the snapshot block
• If an attacker can accumulate enough governance tokens at the snapshot moment (via borrowed/temporarily acquired tokens), they can override everyone’s preferences
• Even honest holders who never meet the snapshot condition can end up effectively ignored in the vote

Why this works (trade-offs & tokenomics implications):
• Snapshot voting improves gas efficiency and prevents last-second vote manipulation—but it can still be gamed if token acquisition is possible around the snapshot.
• Tokenomics that assume “skin in the game” can fail when voting power becomes transferable/borrowable without constraints.
• If the treasury moves immediately after a successful vote, governance becomes a direct execution pathway for malicious proposals.

Security implications to internalize:
• “I hold tokens, therefore I govern” is not always true—governance power may not reflect long-term commitment.
• Snapshot-only governance is insufficient if governance tokens can be flash-loaned/borrowed or rapidly accumulated.
• The blast radius is usually the treasury: once a malicious proposal passes, execution can be irreversible.

Common mitigations (conceptual):
• Use vote delay + timelock so the community can react after a snapshot-based vote
• Employ stronger anti-flash/anti-borrow controls (e.g., require token lock/age, use non-transferable governance units, or balance-weighting with minimum holding periods)
• Add execution guardrails (multisig, circuit breakers, spender limits, or proposal simulations)
• Consider quorum and “rage quit” / exit-based safeguards if token distribution is manipulable

Bottom line: Governance isn’t just “who votes”—it’s “what vote weight really represents at the snapshot, and how quickly execution follows.”

Question for you: Should DAOs treat voting power as “balance at snapshot” or “long-term stake”? Why?
